# Authentication

JSKIT separates provider-neutral authentication behavior, one selected identity
provider, and the browser authentication surface.

For local authentication:

```bash
npm install @jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-core @jskit-ai/auth-web
```

For Supabase authentication:

```bash
npm install @jskit-ai/auth-provider-supabase-core @jskit-ai/auth-web
```

To sign in through an accounts hub or another OpenID Connect issuer (see
[Sign in through an OIDC issuer](/guide/app-setup/sign-in-through-oidc-issuer)):

```bash
npm install @jskit-ai/auth-provider-oidc-core @jskit-ai/auth-web
```

The dependency graph supplies `@jskit-ai/auth-core`. Do not install two
providers for the same `auth.service` capability.

## Provider ownership

The selected provider owns identity verification and sessions. The application
owns permitted login methods, visible OAuth providers, public routes,
post-login destinations, surface access policy, and secret injection.

Use the `auth/auth-surface` pattern for login, sign-out, reset, guards, profile
placements, HTTP integration, and the managed-preview login. Use
`auth/supabase-auth` for the Supabase environment and configuration shape, and
`auth/oidc-sign-in` for an OpenID Connect issuer.

## Managed-preview login is standard

An application with accounts always includes the managed-preview login, whether
or not anyone asked for it. Adding authentication adds both parts from the
`auth/auth-surface` pattern:

- the committed, executable `tools/preview-identity` from its example, which
  passes `runManagedPreviewIdentityCommand` the preview host's protocol id, the
  hostnames, besides loopback, that the host serves the app on, and the process
  environment;
- its declaration to the preview host in the form that host reads (for a host
  that reads the web `Outputs` target, the pattern's `#### Preview identity`
  block: Command `tools/preview-identity`, the same protocol id, Identity types
  `email` `user-id`, Enabled environment `AUTH_DEV_BYPASS_ENABLED`, Secret
  environment `AUTH_DEV_BYPASS_SECRET`, Runtimes `nodejs`).

The preview host supplies both environment values per run, so a managed
preview can sign its browser in as an existing account. Which accounts it may
use stays the person's choice; the application never creates users for it, and
the exchange is inert without both values.

An application whose browsers get in another way, where the development
login-as route is unreachable, passes `runManagedPreviewIdentityCommand` its own
`exchange`, which signs the preview browser in or out and returns its
Set-Cookie headers; its declaration then names no environment values (see the
`auth/auth-surface` pattern).

## Server boundary

`@jskit-ai/auth-core` exposes the policy, actor, extension, and action contracts.
Protected server operations declare an auth policy; they do not trust a hidden
button or a page-local session check. Other packages extend auth through the
public extension capability rather than replacing the auth service.

## When the app profile is synchronized

With users-core, every signed-in identity has an app profile (a `users` row),
and synchronizing it also ensures the user's settings and runs the profile-sync
lifecycle, where workspaces-core provisions the personal workspace. The
providers synchronize in full at sign-in, registration, account changes and
each session refresh (local auth: when the 15-minute access token has expired).
An ordinary request checks its session as always, then reads the
profile once: it synchronizes in full only when the profile is missing or its
email or display name no longer matches the identity the request carries.

So a name or email changed at the provider shows at the next request, while a
personal workspace, owner membership or settings row deleted while the person
is signed in comes back at their next sign-in or session refresh, not at their
next request. Authorization never rests on those rows: sign-out and revoked
sessions take effect at the next request.

## Sign-in protection

Two limits slow down password guessing, and both are on by default.

**Per client address.** Every auth route that can be abused by repetition
declares a `rateLimit`, which the kernel enforces for each client address. A
request over it is refused with status 429, the code `kernel.http.rateLimited`
(`params.count` is the seconds to wait) and a `Retry-After` header. The
defaults, per minute: `login`, `register`, `registerConfirm`,
`loginOtpRequest` and `loginOtpVerify` 10; `registerConfirmationResend` and
`passwordForgot` 5;
`oauthStart`, `oauthComplete`, `passSignIn`, `passwordRecovery` and `passwordReset` 20;
`devLoginAs` 30. Change one in the application's server configuration;
`false` removes it:

```js
// config/server.js
config.auth = {
  ...config.auth,
  rateLimits: {
    login: { max: 5, timeWindow: "1 minute" },
    oauthStart: false
  }
};
```

A route name auth does not have, or a value that is neither
`{ max, timeWindow }` nor `false`, stops startup. `timeWindow` is milliseconds
or text such as `"30 seconds"` or `"1 hour"`.

The address is Fastify's `request.ip`. Behind a reverse proxy every request
comes from the proxy, so all clients would share one count. The app's
`server.js` creates Fastify with
`trustProxy: resolveTrustedProxies(runtimeEnv)` (from
`@jskit-ai/kernel/server/http`), which reads one setting, `TRUSTED_PROXIES`:
the addresses or ranges of the proxies in front of the server, comma-separated,
in Fastify's `trustProxy` syntax (`10.0.0.5`, `10.0.0.0/24`, `fd00::/8`, or
`loopback`, `linklocal` or `uniquelocal`), for example
`TRUSTED_PROXIES=loopback,10.0.0.5`. Only those proxies' `X-Forwarded-For` (and
`-Host` and `-Proto`) is believed, so each client behind them has its own count
and a client that sends the header itself changes nothing. Without the setting
only a proxy on the same machine (`loopback`) is believed. `true` and hop counts
stop startup, because they believe a header any client can send. Name the
narrowest addresses that are only your proxies: a private range shared with
other machines lets each of them choose its address.

**Per account (local auth).** After 5 failed sign-ins in a row for one email,
that email must wait 30 seconds before its next attempt; each further failure
doubles the wait, up to an hour (NIST SP 800-63B's example). While it waits,
sign-in is refused, even with the right password, with status 429, the code
`auth.local.login.locked` (`params.count` minutes, `params.retryAfterSeconds`)
and `Retry-After`. Emails without an account are counted the same way, so the
wait says nothing about which accounts exist. A successful sign-in forgets the
failures, and so does a day without one. Waits are temporary and password
recovery is never blocked: completing a password reset ends the wait, so an
attacker who keeps an account waiting cannot keep its owner out. The failures
are kept in the file store (`sign-in-failures.passwd`) or, with
`@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-db-core`, in the `auth_local_sign_in_failures`
table (run `npm run db:migrate`).

| Env | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTH_LOCAL_SIGN_IN_FAILURES_BEFORE_WAIT` | `5` | Failed sign-ins in a row before the account waits, 1 to 100. |
| `AUTH_LOCAL_SIGN_IN_FIRST_WAIT_SECONDS` | `30` | The first wait. |
| `AUTH_LOCAL_SIGN_IN_MAX_WAIT_SECONDS` | `3600` | The longest wait, at least the first. |
| `AUTH_LOCAL_PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH` | `8` | The shortest password local auth accepts, 8 to 64. |

NIST SP 800-63B-4 asks for at least 15 characters when a password is the only
sign-in factor, and at least 8 when it is used with another factor; set
`AUTH_LOCAL_PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH=15` for password-only sign-in. Passwords up to
128 characters are accepted.

The login page shows either refusal, translated, with the wait.

## Sign-in cookies and SameSite

Local auth's cookies (access, refresh, recovery and OAuth attempt) and
auth-core's CSRF cookie are httpOnly, at `Path=/`, and in production Secure
with the `__Host-` prefix. One setting gives them all their SameSite:

| Env | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTH_COOKIE_SAME_SITE` | `lax` | `lax` or `strict`, letter case and spaces aside. Any other value, `none` included, stops startup, naming the setting. |

`lax` sends the cookies with a top-level navigation that another site starts,
such as a link in a webmail page; `strict` keeps them off every request
another site starts. A site is the scheme and registrable domain, so
applications on sibling subdomains of one registrable domain are one site and
their requests carry the cookies either way; the `__Host-` prefix is what
stops a sibling from setting them.

With `strict`, a page opened from another site loads without the cookies, and
its own requests then carry them, so it shows the person signed in. An
application's JSKIT server sends every page the same, whatever its cookies;
only `/api` requests read the session. Sign-in through Google, Microsoft or
GitHub keeps working: the provider's cross-site return to `/auth/login` only
loads the login page, and the attempt cookie is read by that page's own
`POST /api/oauth/complete`, a same-origin request, which carries Strict
cookies. What `strict` does change: an `/api` GET route that a link on another
site opens directly, such as a download, gets no session.

With the Supabase or OIDC provider the setting applies to the CSRF cookie only;
those providers' own cookies stay `Lax`.

## Second factor (local auth)

Local auth offers a second factor: codes from an authenticator app (TOTP,
RFC 6238), with ten single-use recovery codes for a person who loses the app.
Each account has at most one authenticator. Requiring it is the application's
choice, route by route or role by role; nothing asks for it by default.
OIDC and Supabase sign-in answer `AUTH_OPERATION_UNSUPPORTED`, and
`features.secondFactor` in the auth capabilities is false there.

**Setting it up.** In production, set `AUTH_LOCAL_SECOND_FACTOR_KEY` to a
random secret of at least 32 characters, and `APP_PUBLIC_URL`, whose host the
authenticator app shows beside the codes; without the key a production server
has no second factor. Outside production the session secret stands in for the
key. The key seals each account's authenticator secret (AES-256-GCM, bound to
the account) and keys the hashes of its recovery codes, so keep it: a factor
sealed under one key does not open under another, and verifying it then fails
as a server error until the factor is reset. With
`@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-db-core`, run `npm run db:migrate` (the
`auth_local_second_factors` table and the sessions' `second_factor_at`
column); the file store keeps factors in `second-factors.passwd`.

**Asking for it.** A route asks with `secondFactor`, beside `auth: "required"`
(or `"own"`): `true` for a second factor proved at any time in the session,
`{ maxAgeSeconds }` for one proved that recently, for a dangerous action. A
session that has not proved it is refused, after its CSRF token, sign-in and
permission pass, with 403 `auth.secondFactor.required` (`params.maxAgeSeconds`
when the route names one):

```js
router.register("GET", "/api/console/accounts", { auth: "required", permission: "console.read", secondFactor: true }, listAccounts);
router.register("POST", "/api/console/refunds", { auth: "required", permission: "console.refund", secondFactor: { maxAgeSeconds: 300 } }, refund);
```

When the requirement depends on more than the route, such as the actor's role,
an action asks for it itself; a call without a request (the server's own code)
is refused too:

```js
import { requireSecondFactor } from "@jskit-ai/auth-core/server/secondFactor";
import { resolveRequest } from "@jskit-ai/kernel/server/actions/actionContributorHelpers";

execute(input, context) {
  if (isStaff(context.actor)) {
    requireSecondFactor(resolveRequest(context), { maxAgeSeconds: 300 });
  }
  // ...
}
```

**What the person does.** `@jskit-ai/auth-web` adds the routes under
`/api/second-factor` and three components, each imported from its own path
under `@jskit-ai/auth-web/client/views/` so that only a page that shows one
loads it (the settings' QR code library included). `SecondFactorSettings`
sets an authenticator up (a QR code and the key as text, shown once, then the
app's first code), shows the recovery codes once (to copy, or to download as
`recovery-codes.txt`), replaces them, and removes the authenticator, each with
a code or a recovery code; an app places it as an account settings section,
whose title names it ("Authenticator app"). It emits `codes-saved` when the
person says they saved a new set of codes, so a page that needs an
authenticator before it goes on, such as a console's way in, goes on then.
`SecondFactorPrompt` proves the session's second factor on a page of the app's.
For a route that asks for a recent code, `useSecondFactorStepUp()` runs the
request, and when it is refused with `auth.secondFactor.required` opens
`SecondFactorDialog` and runs it again after the code; cancelling throws the
refusal to the caller. The dialog gives focus back to the element that had it
when it opened (the control that sent the request), after the code as after a
cancel:

```vue
<script setup>
import { useSecondFactorStepUp } from "@jskit-ai/auth-web/client";
import SecondFactorDialog from "@jskit-ai/auth-web/client/views/SecondFactorDialog";

const { open, run, verified, cancel } = useSecondFactorStepUp();
const refund = () => run(() => api.refund(orderId));
</script>

<template>
  <v-btn @click="refund">Refund</v-btn>
  <SecondFactorDialog :open="open" @verified="verified" @cancel="cancel" />
</template>
```

`isSecondFactorRequired(error)` from `@jskit-ai/auth-core/shared/authSecondFactor`
tells that refusal apart elsewhere, such as a page that asks for the second
factor before it shows anything.

**Codes.** A code is accepted within one 30-second step either side of the
server's clock, and only once: no code of an accepted step or an earlier one
passes again (`auth.local.secondFactor.codeUsed`). Wrong codes make the
account wait as failed sign-ins do, counted apart from them under the same
`AUTH_LOCAL_SIGN_IN_*` settings: by default, after five the account waits 30
seconds, doubling up to an hour (429 `auth.local.secondFactor.locked`,
`params.count` minutes). Each route also
has a per-address limit (`secondFactorSetup`, `secondFactorSetupConfirm` and
`secondFactorVerify` 10 a minute, `secondFactorRecoveryCodes` and
`secondFactorRemove` 5), set like the sign-in limits above. Removing the
authenticator ends the second factor of every session of the account.

**Owners and audit.** An owner whose staff lost their authenticator resets it
from the application's own screen: `auth.service`'s
`resetSecondFactor({ userId, byUserId })` removes the account's factor and its
recovery codes, and `listSecondFactors({ userIds })` says which accounts have
one. Who may do either is the application's decision. Every change and every
failed attempt is an event (`setupStarted`, `setupConfirmed`, `verified`,
`failed` with its `reason`, `recoveryCodesReplaced`, `removed`, `reset`) with
the account id, the request's address and the time, never a secret or a code;
an application that keeps an audit log installs the
`auth.local.second-factor-events` capability, a function given each event after
it is stored. Without one, local auth logs them.

## Email confirmation (local auth)

Local auth confirms the email address of each account it registers by
password, in every environment, unless `AUTH_LOCAL_EMAIL_CONFIRMATION=false`.
Two registrations whose email is already proven sign in at once instead: one
through an invitation that a feature's invitation context resolver (such as
workspace invites) resolves, still pending, for the registering email (letter
case aside) and before its `expiresAt`, since its link reached that address;
and the first account a production server's setup code admits (see below). An
invitation passed through as given, with no resolver installed, or whose
context names no email, proves nothing. Any other registration keeps waiting,
with no account, profile or session, and answers
`requiresEmailConfirmation: true`; the sign-in page then
shows "Confirm your email", with a button to send a new link and a field for
the link or its code. Confirming takes the link's code and the password the
registration was made with (`POST /api/register/confirm` with
`{ token, password }`): opening the link (`/auth/login?confirmation_token=...`)
asks for that password, and right after registering the page keeps the one
just typed. Confirming creates the account and signs the person in. The
`auth.local.user.registered` hook runs then, not on registering. A missing or
wrong password creates nothing and keeps the registration and its link, with
status 400 and `auth.local.register.confirmationPasswordInvalid`. Signing in
with the right password while the registration waits is refused with status
403 and `auth.login.emailUnconfirmed`, and the sign-in page shows how to
confirm; a wrong password is an ordinary failed sign-in. The refusal holds
even after `AUTH_LOCAL_EMAIL_CONFIRMATION=false`, which offers no
confirming: the person registers again.

A link's code is random, kept only as a hash, works once and expires after a
day. Registering the same email again replaces the waiting registration whole
and its link, so a waiting registration never keeps the email from its owner.
Asking for a new link replaces the link and keeps the registration, password
included; it answers the same whether or not a registration waits, and sends
nothing for an expired one. The link proves the email and the password proves
the registration: whoever registers an email, before its owner or after, the
account its link creates has the password of the person who confirms it. A
link its owner never asked for confirms nothing with the owner's password;
the owner registers instead.

The link is emailed by the optional `auth.local.confirmation-sender`
capability, an async function accepting `{ email, confirmationUrl }`, built
like the recovery sender below; with it, `APP_PUBLIC_URL` is required and the
link is never returned or logged. In development without one, the link is in
the registration's answer (`confirmationUrl`) and the log, and the sign-in page
shows it with a button that confirms it with the password typed. In production (`NODE_ENV=production`)
without one, while anyone may register, the server refuses to start, naming
the ways out: install a sender, set `AUTH_LOCAL_EMAIL_CONFIRMATION=false`, or
set `AUTH_LOCAL_SELF_REGISTRATION=false`. For direct library
composition, pass the sender as `confirmationSender` to
`createLocalAuthService()`, with `emailConfirmationSender: true` in
`resolveLocalAuthConfig()`; without one, pass
`createLoggedConfirmationSender(logger)`.

In a test copy (`SIDE_EFFECTS` is not `live`, see
[Side effects and test copies](/guide/framework/side-effects)), local auth puts
its own simulated sender in place of an installed
`auth.local.confirmation-sender`, whatever that sender does: it sends nothing,
logs each link for the person testing, and keeps the link out of the answer.
The application's sender never runs there, so no code may depend on it having
run, such as code that confirms a registration with the link its sender was
given: in a test copy that code gets no link.

An application that confirms new accounts at once while its email isn't set up
says so with the optional `auth.local.confirmation-mode` capability, a function
that receives `{ email }` for each registration that would wait for its link
and answers `"link"` (send the link, as without the capability) or
`"without-link"` (create the account and sign the person in at once, as a
confirmed registration does, with the `auth.local.user.registered` hook). The
account it creates has an address nobody proved, so answer `"without-link"`
only when the application accepts that. Any other answer means `"link"` and
logs a warning. Local auth asks only while email confirmation is on and the
address isn't proven already (an invitation or the first account's setup
code). The mode sends nothing, so a test copy keeps it and registers as the
live copy does, while the sender is still replaced. It does not stand in for a
sender: a production server still needs one, or
`AUTH_LOCAL_EMAIL_CONFIRMATION=false`, and `"link"` registrations are sent
through it. An application that never sends a link sets
`AUTH_LOCAL_EMAIL_CONFIRMATION=false` instead.

```js
import { defineProvider } from "@jskit-ai/kernel/shared/capabilities";

// Beside the application's confirmation sender, which emails the link once email is set up.
export const ConfirmationModeProvider = defineProvider({
  id: "app.confirmation-mode",
  requires: { mail: "app.mail" },
  provides: { confirmationMode: "auth.local.confirmation-mode" },
  /** @param {{ mail: import("@local/mail/server/types").AppMail }} capabilities */
  setup({ mail }) {
    /** @type {import("@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-core/server/types").AuthLocalConfirmationMode} */
    async function confirmationMode() {
      return (await mail.isSetUp()) ? "link" : "without-link";
    }
    return { confirmationMode };
  }
});
```

For direct library composition, pass it as `confirmationMode` to
`createLocalAuthService()`.

| Env | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTH_LOCAL_EMAIL_CONFIRMATION` | on | `false` registers and signs in at once, without confirming the email. |
| `AUTH_LOCAL_SELF_REGISTRATION` | on | `false`: only invited accounts and the first account register; anyone else is refused with 403 `auth.local.register.closed`. |

Confirmation guards self-registration. An app whose accounts are only invited,
or created through the first account, sets `AUTH_LOCAL_SELF_REGISTRATION=false`
and needs no confirmation sender: an invitation counts when a feature's
invitation context resolver (such as workspace invites) resolves it for that
email, and the first account is admitted by its setup code. Those
registrations sign in at once, with or without a sender, except an invitation
whose resolver names no email, which confirms when a sender is installed. An
app that refused the register routes itself, with a 404 hook,
can drop the hook for this setting. The sign-in page then shows its Register
tab only to an invited person (an `invitationToken` in its address) and, while
the app has no account, to the first one: local auth reports
`features.password.selfRegister: false` otherwise, and a provider that doesn't
report it offers registering whenever it supports it.

Accounts that exist already are confirmed: only registrations made after the
upgrade wait. Waiting registrations are kept in the file store
(`registrations.passwd`) or, with `@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-db-core`, in
the `auth_local_registrations` table (run `npm run db:migrate`). A custom
`auth.local.backend` implements the `registrations` collection. Tests that
register and expect a session either confirm with the answer's
`confirmationUrl` and the password they registered with, or set
`AUTH_LOCAL_EMAIL_CONFIRMATION=false`.

## Local accounts from application code (database backend)

Application code that works with local auth's records beside local auth, such
as an emailed sign-in link or a job that removes old sessions, requires their
owners' capabilities from `@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-db-core` and never
reads or writes the `auth_local_*` tables. Every method takes the call's
`options` last and runs in `options.trx` when there is one. That transaction
must be a managed one: open it with one of the application's own table
resource handles, `handle.withTransaction(options, (txOptions) => …)`, and pass
`txOptions` on. Their writes refuse a transaction from `knex.transaction()`, and
a failed write fails the whole transaction even when the work catches its
error.

| Capability | Methods |
| --- | --- |
| `auth.local.accounts` | `create(account, options)`, `findById(userId, options)`, `findByEmail(email, options)`, `updatePassword(userId, passwordRecord, options)`, `updateProfile(userId, { displayName }, options)`, `markEmailVerified(userId, options)` |
| `auth.local.sessions` | `create(session, options)`, `update(sessionId, { purpose, expiresAt }, { ...options, onlyIf })`, `revoke(sessionId, options)`, `revokeForUser(userId, { ...options, exceptSessionId })`, `deleteExpired(now, options)` |
| `auth.local.recovery` | `create(token, options)`, `findByTokenHash(tokenHash, options)`, `consume(tokenId, options)`, `consumeForUser(userId, { ...options, idPrefix })` |

`markEmailVerified` records that the account proved it owns its email address,
for example by using an emailed link, in the `email_verified_at` column (run
`npm run db:migrate`); the first proof is kept, and the account answers it as
`emailVerifiedAt` (empty until then). `deleteExpired` deletes the sessions that
expired by `now` and answers how many.

A recovery token's kind is the start of its id: local sign-in's password resets
are `rec_…`, and an app's own kind (a sign-in link, say) takes a prefix of its
own, such as `magic_…`. `consumeForUser` consumes the user's open tokens of the
kind `idPrefix` names and no others, so a new sign-in link leaves an open
password reset usable, and a completed reset leaves sign-in links open.
`update` with `onlyIf` (`userId`, `purpose`, `revokedAt`) changes the session
only while it still has those values, compared in the UPDATE itself, and
answers null, writing nothing, when it does not: promote a sign-in link's
session with
`update(sessionId, { purpose: "normal", expiresAt }, { ...options, onlyIf: { userId, purpose: "recovery", revokedAt: null } })`
and treat null as a refused link. Their types are `AuthLocalAccounts`,
`AuthLocalSessions` and `AuthLocalRecovery` in
`@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-db-core/server/types`.

## The first account in production (local auth)

The first account to register becomes the application's owner, so on a
production server (`NODE_ENV=production`) whose local auth has no account yet,
registering needs a one-time setup code that only the server's operator can
read. Development needs no code.

Each start of such a server makes a new code, such as
`7KQ2M-X9D4F-0RWHN-3TBZC`, and keeps only its hash. It writes the code:

- in the log, as one warning: `Local auth has no account yet: register the
  first account with this setup code.`, with the fields
  `firstAccountSetupCode` (the code) and `firstAccountSetupCodeFile`;
- in the file `first-account-setup-code` in `AUTH_LOCAL_STORE_DIR` (default
  `.jskit/auth`), mode 600, for a hosting tool to read. A store directory that
  cannot be written leaves only the log line.

While it waits, the sign-in page's registration form shows a "Setup code"
field (capability `features.firstAccountSetupCode`), and the register body
takes `setupCode`; letter case, spaces and dashes do not matter. A missing code
is refused with 403 `auth.local.setup.codeRequired`, a wrong one with 403
`auth.local.setup.codeInvalid`. An OAuth sign-in cannot create that first
account. The registration then follows the ordinary rules, except that it
needs no email confirmation: only the operator can read the code, so it signs
the owner in at once. The code admits registrations
until an account exists; then it stops working and its file is deleted, and
registration needs no code again. Restarting before then makes a new code and
the old one stops working: the latest log line and the file always agree, and
nothing but a hash is kept for checking it. Run one server while the first
account is set up, since each server makes its own code.

A hosting tool that shows the code to the operator itself supplies it in
`AUTH_LOCAL_SETUP_CODE`, at least 20 letters and digits, for example a
generated production secret. The server then asks for that code at every start
and on every server, writes no `first-account-setup-code` file, and logs only
that the code is in `AUTH_LOCAL_SETUP_CODE`, never the code itself. Outside
production the variable is ignored.

## One-time pass sign-in (local auth)

An application whose people already signed in somewhere else, such as a
hosting site that opens each person's own server, can let that site sign them
in with no second password. The site, the issuer, signs a pass with its
Ed25519 private key; the application holds only the public key. A pass names
one person (`sub`), the application it is for (`aud`), one resource of that
application (`resource`, such as the one server it runs on) and its own id
(`jti`), and lasts a minute. The person's browser posts it to the application,
which signs in the account the pass names, once.

Three settings turn it on; without the key nothing changes: there is no pass
route and password sign-in stays as it is.

| Env | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `AUTH_PASS_PUBLIC_KEY` | The issuer's Ed25519 public key: a PEM block, or its base64 DER on one line (the PEM body without its header lines). |
| `AUTH_PASS_AUDIENCE` | The application every pass must name, such as `editor`. Required with the key. |
| `AUTH_PASS_RESOURCE` | The one resource every pass must name, such as this server's name. Required with the key. |

The application says which account a pass signs in with the
`auth.local.pass-identity` capability, a function given the verified pass
(`{ id, subject, audience, resource, issuedAt, expiresAt, usableUntil }`) that
answers the local account's id, or null when its subject has none here. With
the key set and no mapping installed, startup stops saying so.

```js
import { defineProvider } from "@jskit-ai/kernel/shared/capabilities";

export const PassIdentityProvider = defineProvider({
  id: "app.pass-identity",
  requires: { accounts: "auth.local.accounts" },
  provides: { passIdentity: "auth.local.pass-identity" },
  /** @param {{ accounts: import("@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-db-core/server/types").AuthLocalAccounts }} capabilities */
  setup({ accounts }) {
    /** @type {import("@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-core/server/types").AuthLocalPassIdentity} */
    async function passIdentity(pass) {
      // This issuer names each person by the email of their account here.
      return (await accounts.findByEmail(pass.subject))?.id ?? null;
    }
    return { passIdentity };
  }
});
```

For direct library composition, pass it as `passIdentity` to
`createLocalAuthService()`, whose `signInWithPass({ pass })` signs in and
answers as `login` does.

The browser posts the pass as the form field `pass` to `POST /api/login/pass`,
from a page of the issuer's that submits itself, so the pass never sits in an
address, a history or a log:

```html
<form method="post" action="https://app.example.com/api/login/pass">
  <input type="hidden" name="pass" value="PASS">
</form>
<script>document.forms[0].submit();</script>
```

A pass that signs in sets the session cookies and answers `303` to `/`. The pass
authenticates the post, so the route takes no CSRF token, and it is limited per
client address like the other sign-in routes (`passSignIn`, 20 a minute). A
refused pass answers `303` to `/auth/login` with `error=sign_in_unavailable`,
the reason in `error_description` and its code in `error_code`, and the sign-in
page shows the reason:

| Code | Status | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auth.pass.malformed` | 401 | Not a pass, issued over 30 seconds ahead of this server's clock, or meant to last over five minutes. |
| `auth.pass.badSignature` | 401 | Not signed by the issuer's key, or changed after signing. |
| `auth.pass.wrongAudience` | 401 | For another application. |
| `auth.pass.wrongResource` | 401 | For another resource. |
| `auth.pass.expired` | 401 | Expired (30 seconds of clock difference are allowed). |
| `auth.pass.replayed` | 401 | Already used, on this server or another sharing its store. |
| `auth.pass.unmapped` | 403 | The mapping names no account, or a disabled one. |

Each pass signs in once. Local auth records each pass it accepts, by the hash
of its id, until it could no longer be used anyway (30 seconds after it
expired), before it asks the mapping: an unmapped pass is used up too. The
database backend keeps them in `auth_local_used_passes` (run
`npm run db:migrate`), so every server on the database refuses a pass another
accepted; the file backend keeps them in `passes.passwd` in its store. A pass
signs in an ordinary session: it does not prove a second factor, which a route
that asks for one still asks for.

The pass itself is `@jskit-ai/auth-pass`, a package that installs no providers.
The issuer signs passes with `signPass` from `@jskit-ai/auth-pass/server`, or
with any JOSE library: a pass is a compact JWS with the header
`{ "alg": "EdDSA", "typ": "pass+jwt" }` and the claims above plus `iat` and
`exp`, in seconds.

```js
import { signPass } from "@jskit-ai/auth-pass/server";

// On the issuer's server, which alone holds the private key (a KeyObject or PEM).
const pass = signPass({ privateKey, subject: "ada@example.com", audience: "editor", resource: "machine-7" });
```

Make the key pair with
`openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out pass-issuer.pem`, and the public key
the application is given with
`openssl pkey -in pass-issuer.pem -pubout`. The application trusts one key: to
change it, the issuer starts signing with the new key as the application
starts with it, and passes signed with the old key are refused. A person who
holds a valid pass of their own could post it from another person's browser
and sign that browser in as themselves, as with any sign-in link, so an issuer
signs passes only for its signed-in person, just before posting them.

An application with a sign-in of its own, not local auth, checks passes with
`@jskit-ai/auth-pass/server` alone. Depending on it installs nothing, while
depending on auth-core would install auth-core's auth policy, CSRF and auth
actions in that application. `resolvePassSignInFromEnv(env)` reads the same
three settings (null without the key). `verifyPass(token, settings)` answers
the verified pass or throws one of the refusals above. Single use and the
mapping are then the application's: it records `pass.id` until
`pass.usableUntil` and throws `createPassError(PASS_TEXTS.passReplayed)` for a
pass it saw before, then `createPassError(PASS_TEXTS.passUnmapped)` for a
subject it does not know.

## Application-owned recovery email

Local auth owns recovery tokens, expiry and recovery-scoped sessions. The
application supplies the optional `auth.local.recovery-sender` capability as an
async function accepting `{ email, recoveryUrl }`. It owns message content,
sender address, provider credentials and delivery. The function must reject on
failure and must not log the recovery URL or raw provider credentials.

Wire the application's selected email integration or transport into this
capability using an ordinary application provider:

```js
import { defineProvider } from "@jskit-ai/kernel/shared/capabilities";
import { createRecoverySender } from "./recoverySender.js";

export const RecoveryEmailProvider = defineProvider({
  id: "app.recovery-email",
  requires: { mail: "app.mail" },
  provides: { recoverySender: "auth.local.recovery-sender" },
  /** @param {{ mail: import("@local/mail/server/types").AppMail }} capabilities */
  setup({ mail }) {
    return { recoverySender: createRecoverySender({ mail }) };
  }
});
```

```js
// recoverySender.js
/** @param {{ mail: import("@local/mail/server/types").AppMail }} dependencies */
function createRecoverySender({ mail }) {
  /** @type {import("@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-core/server/types").AuthLocalRecoverySender} */
  async function sendRecoveryEmail({ email, recoveryUrl }) {
    await mail.send({
      to: email,
      subject: "Reset your password",
      text: `Open this link to reset your password:\n\n${recoveryUrl}\n`
    });
  }

  return sendRecoveryEmail;
}

export { createRecoverySender };
```

`app.mail` is an application-owned capability in this example, not a built-in
JSKIT email API. Its `send()` implementation owns the selected integration,
credential resolution and safe error mapping. A connected account or a domain
listing adapter alone does not implement email sending. Install this provider
alongside the application's mail provider and `AuthLocalProvider`.
[Typed features](/guide/framework/typed-features) describes how application
providers name and type the capabilities they receive.
For direct library composition, pass the same function as `recoverySender` to
`createLocalAuthService()`, with a configuration from
`resolveLocalAuthConfig({ appRoot, env, fileBackend, emailRecovery: true })`.

Set `APP_PUBLIC_URL` to the application's actual public URL. When a sender is
configured, auth requires this value and does not return or log the recovery
URL. Without a sender, production recovery is disabled; explicit development
output remains available for local testing. A sender failure never falls back
to development output. The generic recovery delivery capability is `email`.

The sender runs after the request has answered. Asking for a password reset
answers at once, and the same, whether or not the email has an account, so
neither the answer nor its time tells anyone which emails have accounts: local
auth looks the account up, makes its link and calls the sender only once the
request has answered. When the sender rejects, local auth logs the failure
with the address (never the link), and the person sees the same answer as for
any email; a delivery failure someone must act on belongs in the sender's own
monitoring, since an answer that reported it would say the account exists. A
stopping server waits up to 10 seconds for the emails still being sent. Asking
for a new confirmation link (`resendRegisterConfirmation`) and the
`auth.local.confirmation-sender` work the same way; a new registration's link
is still sent before its answer, which already says whether the email is
taken. A test that composes the library directly and reads the sent email
waits for it: it passes `deliveries: createLocalDeliveries({ logger })` to
`createLocalAuthService()` and awaits `deliveries.settled()`.

Production is `NODE_ENV=production`; anything else, unset included, is
development, so the host that serves the application sets it. A production
server with `AUTH_LOCAL_RECOVERY_DEV_OUTPUT` set refuses to start and names the
setting to remove, rather than ignoring it.

### Pre-release migration

This is a V0 breaking change. There is one runtime path, with no old SMTP reader
or compatibility adapter.

1. Supply `auth.local.recovery-sender` (or the direct `recoverySender` argument)
   using your application’s chosen delivery implementation.
2. Move sender, reply-to and transport credentials into that implementation's
   configuration and private Env. Remove `AUTH_LOCAL_SMTP_HOST`,
   `AUTH_LOCAL_SMTP_PORT`, `AUTH_LOCAL_SMTP_SECURE`, `AUTH_LOCAL_SMTP_USER`,
   `AUTH_LOCAL_SMTP_PASSWORD`, `AUTH_LOCAL_SMTP_FROM` and
   `AUTH_LOCAL_SMTP_REPLY_TO`. These variables are no longer consumed by auth.
3. If retaining SMTP, explicitly install Nodemailer in the application and own
   its transport there. Local auth no longer installs or imports Nodemailer.
4. Retain `APP_PUBLIC_URL`. Replace direct-service `config.smtp` and
   `config.smtpConfigured` with the sender argument. Update consumers that
   inspect `features.passwordRecovery.delivery` from `smtp` to `email`, including
   Supabase-backed consumers: this describes delivery, not transport protocol.
5. Verify recovery delivery, unknown-account responses, delivery failures and
   the completed password-reset flow before releasing the updated application.
   This change does not alter identity, session or recovery-token storage.

## Google, Microsoft and GitHub sign-in with local auth

Local auth signs people in through Google, Microsoft and GitHub when the
application sets each provider's client id and secret in private Env:

| Provider | Env pair | Protocol and scopes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Google | `AUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`, `AUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET` | OpenID Connect discovery, `openid email profile` |
| Microsoft | `AUTH_MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID`, `AUTH_MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET` | OpenID Connect discovery through the `common` endpoint, `openid email profile` |
| GitHub | `AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID`, `AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET` | OAuth 2.0, `read:user user:email`, email from `GET /user/emails` |

A provider appears in `oauthLogin.providers` only when both values of its pair
are set; setting one without the other stops startup. `APP_PUBLIC_URL` is then
required, and every provider's app registration must allow exactly
`${APP_PUBLIC_URL}/auth/login` as its redirect address. The login page posts the
callback to `/api/oauth/complete`, which completes the provider the attempt
started with.

Register the Microsoft app for accounts in any organizational directory and
personal Microsoft accounts, and add the optional ID token claim `xms_edov`.

Security behavior:

- The authorization-code flow uses PKCE (`S256`) and `state`, plus `nonce` for
  OpenID Connect. The attempt is stored server-side, in the file store or the
  `auth_local_oauth_attempts` table, under the hash of a random httpOnly
  `jskit_local_oauth_attempt` cookie (`__Host-` in production, SameSite from
  `AUTH_COOKIE_SAME_SITE`; see
  [Sign-in cookies and SameSite](#sign-in-cookies-and-samesite)), so it
  completes only in the starting browser and works across several servers. It
  is deleted when used and expires after ten minutes.
- ID tokens are verified against the provider's JWKS: signature, issuer,
  audience, expiry and nonce.
- Only a verified email signs in: Google's `email_verified`, GitHub's primary
  verified address, and for Microsoft a personal account or a work or school
  account whose token carries `xms_edov: true`. A Microsoft token without an
  email claim is refused.
- `returnTo` must be on the application's own origin; anything else returns to
  `/`.

A sign-in matches the provider subject first. Otherwise a verified email that
matches an existing user signs that user in and links the provider identity,
and a new email creates the user the way `register` does: the
`auth.local.user.registered` hook runs and profile synchronization provisions
the personal workspace. An account created this way has no password until
password recovery sets one. Sessions are ordinary local sessions; provider
tokens are discarded after sign-in.

With providers configured, the `providerLinking` capability is on. The security
status lists each provider as an `oauth:<provider>` method, where `canEnable`
means it can be linked and `canDisable` that it can be unlinked.
`GET /api/settings/security/oauth/:provider/start` links a provider to the
signed-in account and `DELETE /api/settings/security/oauth/:provider` unlinks
it. Unlinking the last sign-in method is refused, and so is linking an identity
that already belongs to another account. The `users/account-settings` pattern's
sign-in methods section offers both.

With `@jskit-ai/auth-provider-local-db-core`, run `npm run db:migrate` to create
the `auth_local_identities` and `auth_local_oauth_attempts` tables.

## Browser boundary

`@jskit-ai/auth-web` owns the normal auth views, guard runtime, sign-out flow,
and auth-aware HTTP integration. `DefaultLoginView`, `DefaultResetPasswordView`
and `DefaultSignOutView` fill the window themselves: a card on
`surface-container` on wide windows, the whole screen on phones, and each
screen's one `h1` ("Sign in", "Create your account", "Reset password", ...).
Every app shows its identity there, so a person always sees which app they are
signing in to. It goes in their `brand` slot, which JSKIT lays out: a pane
beside the card on wide windows (`primary-container`, its children from top to
bottom) and a compact row above the card on phones. The slot gets `{ compact }`
to choose what to show, and holds no heading. The `auth/auth-surface` pattern
does this already: its pages render the app's view wrappers
(`src/views/auth/LoginView.vue`, `ResetPasswordView.vue`, `SignOutView.vue`),
and each fills the slot with `src/components/AppBrand.vue`, the app's name as
`index.html`'s `<title>` spells it. Renaming the app renames both:

```vue
<template>
  <DefaultLoginView>
    <template #brand="{ compact }">
      <AppBrand :compact="compact" />
    </template>
  </DefaultLoginView>
</template>
```

An app with a logo or a line about the product puts them in `AppBrand.vue`
too, keeping the name.

Never restyle the views' own classes (`.login-screen`, `.auth-card`) or wrap
them in a frame of the app's; the brand slot is the one way in.

Initial load errors stay inside the affected surface. Failed login, reset, and
other transient mutations use the application toast and do not shift the form.
Loading uses skeletons when content geometry is known.

## Verification

Test successful and failed registration/login, sign-out, password reset,
protected direct navigation, return destinations, refresh, expired sessions,
and negative cross-origin behavior. For Supabase, also exercise callback and
refresh flows.

For direct localhost Playwright tests, enable the development auth bypass only
in the server process and use `loginAsExistingUser()` from
`@jskit-ai/auth-web/test/playwright`. The Node-side helper sends the private
`x-jskit-dev-auth-secret`; never pass that secret through browser code, URLs, or
client environment. Under `browserTestConfig()`, a `signIn` module signs each
worker in once with `loginRequestAsExistingUser()` instead of each test
signing in ([Upgrading JSKIT](/guide/app-setup/upgrading-jskit#sign-each-browser-worker-in-once)).

A managed host instead supplies authenticated state through
`PLAYWRIGHT_STORAGE_STATE` and the app-owned Playwright config. Treat the
file as a temporary secret, use relative URLs, and do not call the localhost
login helper or start a duplicate server.

The login state belongs to the host, which already fits it to the tested site.
Pass `process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_STORAGE_STATE` unchanged to `use.storageState`:
the config never reads, parses or edits that file or its `cookies` or
`origins`. `jskit/playwright-login-unchanged` reports a config that does, and
the host refuses to run its tests. If tests run signed out with the unchanged
state, that is a host defect: report it with the evidence; do not work around
it.

Never commit provider secrets, copy auth repositories into the app, or add an
installation questionnaire, mutation record, or setup receipt.
